              ‘We missed it’: Amitabh Kant says CAFE III should have made EVs the destination

              Former NITI Aayog CEO says multiple compliance pathways dilute the push towards electrification; also questions BEE’s role in credit mechanism

              By Amit Vijay Mohile

              Updated - September 30, 2026 at 12:30 PM.
              ×

              Share

              WhatsAppXFacebookLinkedInMessengerRedditMail
              https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/we-missed-it-amitabh-kant-says-cafe-iii-should-have-made-evs-the-destination/article71527151.ece

              Amitabh Kant | Photo Credit: RAVINDRAN R

              Listen to audio version of this article
              Sponsored by
              0:00 / 2:23
              Instaread

              India missed an opportunity to make electric vehicles the clear destination of its new fuel-efficiency regime, former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant said, arguing that the final CAFE III norms instead give carmakers multiple routes — including hybrids, ethanol, CNG and efficiency credits to meet their targets, while also questioning the Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s role in administering a mechanism to address compliance shortfalls.

              “This was the moment to pole vault. We missed it,” Kant said after the Ministry of Power notified the final Corporate Average Fuel Economy norms.

              “EVs become one option among many when they should be the destination,” he said. “The regulation follows the industry instead of leading it.”

              Technology-neutral approach

              Kant’s objection goes to the basic design of CAFE III. The government has chosen what it calls a “future-ready, technology-neutral and flexible regulatory framework”, allowing manufacturers to decide how they meet progressively tougher fuel-efficiency targets.

              Battery and range-extended EVs receive the highest 3x volume multiplier, but they are not the only technologies rewarded. Plug-in hybrids and flex-fuel strong hybrids get 2.5x, conventional strong hybrids 1.6x, and flex-fuel ethanol vehicles 1.1x.

              Biofuels provide another route. Flex-fuel ethanol vehicles receive a 22.3 per cent carbon-neutrality factor, eligible E20-or-higher petrol vehicles get 8 per cent and CNG gets at least 5 per cent.

              The government says these alternatives are deliberate, describing biofuels as an “additional pathway” for improving fleet-level CAFE performance alongside vehicle-efficiency improvements and electrification.

              Kant’s argument is that India should have gone further. With the country heavily dependent on imported oil while simultaneously building battery and EV manufacturing capacity, he says regulation should steer automakers towards electrification rather than leave EVs competing with several other compliance pathways.

              “The headline stringency is real, but the flexibilities stack up,” Amit Bhatt, Managing Director, International Council on Clean Transportation, said separately.

              BEE role questioned:

              Kant has also challenged the compliance-credit mechanism. “How can BEE sell credits? A regulator can’t be a player in the market it regulates,” he said.

              The final framework allows manufacturers facing compliance gaps to use eligible carried-forward credits, trade credits with other manufacturers or use a buyout mechanism administered by BEE.

              For Kant, the dispute therefore is not simply about how tough CAFE III is. It is about where the regulation is intended to take India’s automobile industry. “This was the moment to pole vault,” he said. “We missed it.”

              Published on September 30, 2026
